title: Python
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: The flood has drained away, and the earth, still warm and muddy, breeds again of herself — this part is Ovid's account of spontaneous generation, argued in the vocabulary of natural philosophy: seeds, moisture, heat, and the balance struck between them, with the annual silt of the Nile as its standing proof. It sits early in Book I, immediately after Deucalion and Pyrrha have remade humankind by throwing stones behind them. Out of the mud come the old species and new ones besides, among them the serpent Python, sprawling across a mountainside and a terror to the newly made peoples. Apollo, whose bow until now has been for deer and roe, all but empties his quiver into it and founds the Pythian games so that the deed will not be forgotten. The lines close on an absence: there was as yet no laurel, and the god wreathed his head from whatever tree came to hand. The tale that follows is Daphne's, and it is the one that accounts for the laurel.

sentences.t:
Cetera diversis tellus animalia formis
sponte sua peperit, postquam vetus umor ab igne
percaluit solis, caenumque udaeque paludes
intumuere aestu,
sentences.l:
The rest of the living creatures, in differing forms, the earth
of its own accord brought forth, after the old moisture grew hot
from the fire of the sun, and the mud and the sodden marshes
swelled with the heat,
sentences.i: The earth brought forth the remaining living creatures of her own accord, in all their differing shapes, once the ancient moisture had grown hot in the sun's fire and the mud and the sodden marshes swelled with the heat,
sentences.n: 'Cetera… animalia' (the rest of the living creatures) picks up from the stones of Deucalion and Pyrrha, which had just made human beings: everything else the earth produced by itself. 'sponte sua' — 'of its own accord' — is the standing phrase for spontaneous generation, which ancient natural philosophy took for granted. 'intumuere' is 'intumuerunt': the poetic third-person plural perfect in -ēre, extremely common in verse — watch for it throughout this part. 'ab igne… solis' (from the fire of the sun) has its genitive thrown over the line-end, normal in hexameter.

sentences.t:
fecundaque semina rerum
vivaci nutrita solo ceu matris in alvo
creverunt faciemque aliquam cepere morando.
sentences.l:
and the fertile seeds of things,
nourished in the life-giving soil as in a mother's belly,
grew, and took on some shape or other by delaying.
sentences.n: 'semina rerum' — 'the seeds of things' — is the Lucretian phrase for the elemental particles out of which everything is made; Ovid is writing physics here as much as myth. 'vivaci solo' is ablative, the soil itself quick with life, and the comparison 'ceu matris in alvo' (as in a mother's belly) turns the earth into a womb. 'cepere' = 'ceperunt' — the -ēre perfect again. 'morando' is the gerund in the ablative, 'by delaying,' i.e. as time went on.

sentences.t:
Sic ubi deseruit madidos septemfluus agros
Nilus et antiquo sua flumina reddidit alveo
aetherioque recens exarsit sidere limus,
sentences.l:
So, when it has left the sodden fields, seven-streaming
Nile, and has given its own waters back to their ancient bed,
and, by the star of heaven, the fresh slime has blazed hot,
sentences.i: So it is when the seven-mouthed Nile withdraws from the drenched fields and returns its waters to their old channel, and the star of heaven sets the fresh slime blazing:
sentences.n: 'septemfluus' — 'seven-flowing' — is the Nile of the seven mouths of its delta; the annual flood laid down the silt that made Egypt fertile, and antiquity treated that silt as the standard proof that life comes out of mud. 'Nilus' is held back to the head of the next line, so the reader meets the epithet before the river it belongs to. 'aetherio sidere' ('by the heavenly star') is the sun. 'limus' — river slime — is the key word of the whole passage.

sentences.t:
plurima cultores versis animalia glaebis
inveniunt,
sentences.l:
very many living things, the clods once turned,
the farmers find,
sentences.i: the farmers, turning the clods, find a great many living creatures,
sentences.n: 'versis glaebis' is an ablative absolute — a self-contained 'with the clods turned' where English wants a clause ('when they turn the soil'). You will meet this construction constantly. The word order is interlocked: 'plurima… animalia' (very many creatures) is split wide open around 'cultores versis… glaebis,' so the whole line has to be held in suspense until 'inveniunt' resolves it. The present tense is generalising — this is what happens every year, not once.

sentences.i: and among them they see some only just begun, still inside the very passage of birth, others unfinished, maimed in the parts that should have made them whole;
sentences.n: 'nascendi spatium' — 'the span of being born': 'nascendi' is the genitive of the gerund, so literally 'the interval of coming-to-be.' These creatures are caught mid-birth in the mud. 'suis trunca numeris' is the hard phrase: 'numeri' here are the parts or members that make a body complete (the word runs from 'number' through 'limb' to 'rhythm'), so 'cut short in their own numbers' means missing some of what they ought to have had. 'quaedam… quaedam' — 'some… others' — balances the two halves.

sentences.t:
et eodem in corpore saepe
altera pars vivit, rudis est pars altera tellus.
sentences.l:
and in the same body often
one part is alive, the other part is raw earth.
sentences.n: 'altera pars… pars altera' — 'one part… the other part': the two phrases mirror each other in reversed order, so the sentence enacts the split it describes. 'rudis' is 'raw, unworked, unformed,' the word used of untooled timber or clay. The creature is half animal and half still the dirt it is climbing out of.

sentences.t:
Quippe ubi temperiem sumpsere umorque calorque,
concipiunt, et ab his oriuntur cuncta duobus;
sentences.l:
For when moisture and heat have taken on a right blend,
they conceive, and from these two all things arise;
sentences.n: 'temperiem' is the right mixture or proportion — the root of 'temperate.' Ancient physics held that generation happens only when the elements come into balance, and 'concipiunt' ('they conceive') makes moisture and heat the two parents. '-que… -que' in 'umorque calorque' is the poetic 'both… and.' 'sumpsere' = 'sumpserunt': the -ēre perfect once more.

sentences.t:
cumque sit ignis aquae pugnax, vapor umidus omnes
res creat, et discors concordia fetibus apta est.
sentences.l:
and though fire is at war with water, a moist warmth
creates all things, and a discordant concord is fit for breeding.
sentences.i: and though fire makes war on water, it is moist heat that creates everything: a quarrelsome harmony is what suits the getting of offspring.
sentences.n: 'ignis aquae pugnax' — 'fire, fighting-with water': the adjective 'pugnax' takes the dative 'aquae.' 'vapor umidus' is 'moist heat,' steam, the two enemies in union. 'discors concordia' ('discordant concord') is a contradiction folded into two words, the kind of oxymoron Ovid builds whole arguments on; the same paradox — opposites held in tension — governs his account of creation from the poem's opening. 'fetibus apta' is 'suited to offspring,' i.e. good for breeding.

sentences.t:
Ergo ubi diluvio tellus lutulenta recenti
solibus aetheriis altoque recanduit aestu,
edidit innumeras species,
sentences.l:
So when the earth, muddied by the flood just past,
glowed white again with the suns of heaven and the heat from on high,
she gave forth countless kinds,
sentences.n: 'diluvio… recenti' (by the recent flood) is a causal ablative split wide and wrapped around 'tellus lutulenta,' the muddy earth; Deucalion's flood is only a few lines behind us. 'recanduit' carries the prefix 're-': after the water, the earth grows white-hot again. 'solibus' is plural — the sun's repeated days, or its rays — and 'alto… aestu' is heat from on high, matching 'aetheriis'; both are ablatives of means. 'species' here means 'kinds, sorts' of living thing, not 'appearance.'

sentences.t:
partimque figuras
rettulit antiquas, partim nova monstra creavit.
sentences.l:
and in part brought back the ancient shapes,
in part created new monsters.
sentences.n: 'partim… partim' — 'partly… partly' — balanced across the line-end, one half to each side. 'rettulit' (from 'refero') is 'brought back, reproduced': the species that had existed before the flood. 'monstra' is not simply 'monsters': the root is 'monstrare / monere,' a thing shown or a thing warned of, so a 'monstrum' is a portent, an unnatural shape that means something. The next line supplies one.

sentences.t:
Illa quidem nollet, sed te quoque, maxime Python,
tum genuit, populisque novis, incognite serpens,
terror eras: tantum spatii de monte tenebas.
sentences.l:
She would not have wished it, indeed — but you too, greatest Python,
she bore then, and to the new peoples, serpent never known before,
you were a terror: so much of the mountain's space you held.
sentences.i: Not that she wished it — but she bore you too then, mighty Python, and to those new peoples you were a horror, a serpent they had never known: such a stretch of the mountainside you filled.
sentences.n: Ovid turns aside from the story to address the snake directly — 'te… maxime Python… incognite serpens,' with 'eras' and 'tenebas' in the second person. This is apostrophe, the move he makes when a figure deserves the reader's whole attention for a moment. 'Illa quidem nollet' is a potential subjunctive, 'she would not have wished it': the earth breeds Python against her own will. 'tantum spatii' is a partitive genitive, 'so much of space' — and Ovid never says how much, which is the point. Python is the serpent of Delphi; the mountain is Parnassus.

sentences.t:
Hunc deus arquitenens, et numquam talibus armis
ante nisi in dammis capreisque fugacibus usus,
sentences.l:
Him the bow-bearing god — never before having used such weapons
except on does and fleeing roe —
sentences.i: The bow-bearing god, who had never before turned such weapons on anything but does and fleeing roe,
sentences.n: 'arquitenens' — 'bow-holder' — is a cult title of Apollo; the edition keeps the older spelling with -qu-. 'usus' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'utor' (to use), which governs the ablative, hence 'talibus armis.' The object 'hunc' (him, i.e. Python) is thrown to the front and then left hanging for four lines until its verb 'perdidit' finally lands. The aside is pointed: until now Apollo's bow has been a hunting toy. The edition prints 'talibus armis' ('such weapons'); some editions print 'letalibus' ('deadly weapons').

sentences.t:
mille gravem telis exhausta paene pharetra
perdidit effuso per vulnera nigra veneno.
sentences.l:
him, heavy with a thousand shafts — the quiver all but drained —
he destroyed, the venom poured out through the black wounds.
sentences.i: brought him down under a thousand arrows, his quiver all but emptied, the venom running out through the black wounds.
sentences.n: Two ablative absolutes stacked inside two lines: 'exhausta paene pharetra' (with the quiver nearly drained) and 'effuso… veneno' (with the poison poured out). 'gravem' agrees with 'hunc' back at the start of line 441 — it is Python who is 'heavy,' weighted with the shafts standing in him. 'mille' is round-number hyperbole, not a count. 'perdidit' is stronger than 'killed': it is 'destroyed, did away with.'

sentences.t:
Neve operis famam posset delere vetustas,
instituit sacros celebri certamine ludos,
Pythia perdomitae serpentis nomine dictos.
sentences.l:
And lest length of years be able to blot out the fame of the deed,
he founded sacred games with a thronged contest,
called Pythian from the name of the serpent he had mastered.
sentences.i: And so that the passing of years should not blot out the fame of the deed, he founded sacred games, with contests that drew crowds, called Pythian after the name of the serpent he had subdued.
sentences.n: 'neve… posset' is a negative purpose clause — 'and so that age might not be able to…' — which is why 'posset' is subjunctive. 'vetustas' is not old age but the sheer lapse of time, the thing that wears reputations away. These are the Pythian games at Delphi, one of the four great Panhellenic festivals, and Ovid is giving them an origin story — the kind of explanation that runs all through the poem. 'perdomitae' is 'thoroughly tamed,' with the intensive prefix 'per-'.

sentences.t:
Hic iuvenum quicumque manu pedibusve rotave
vicerat, aesculeae capiebat frondis honorem:
sentences.l:
Here, whichever of the young men had won by hand or by foot or by wheel
would take the honour of a leaf of oak:
sentences.i: Here, whichever of the young men had won with his hands, his feet or the wheel carried off the honour of an oak-leaf crown:
sentences.n: 'manu pedibusve rotave' — 'by hand or by feet or by wheel' — names the three kinds of event in a single line: the boxing and wrestling, the foot-races, the chariot. The pluperfect 'vicerat' with the imperfect 'capiebat' makes the whole thing customary: this is what happened at each celebration, year after year. 'aesculea frons' is the leaf of the 'aesculus,' the winter oak sacred to Jupiter — pointedly not the laurel.

sentences.t:
nondum laurus erat, longoque decentia crine
tempora cingebat de qualibet arbore Phoebus.
sentences.l:
the laurel did not yet exist, and his temples, comely with long hair,
Phoebus would wreathe from whatever tree he pleased.
sentences.i: there was as yet no laurel, and Phoebus would bind his temples — handsome beneath their long hair — with leaves from any tree at all.
sentences.n: 'nondum laurus erat' — 'the laurel did not yet exist' — is what the whole aside turns on: Apollo's laurel crown, the most familiar thing about him, has no origin yet, and the tale that comes next, Daphne's, is the one that gives it one. 'decentia' agrees with 'tempora' (his temples); 'longo… crine' is an ablative attached to 'decentia' — comely by reason of the long hair. 'de qualibet arbore' — 'from any tree you like' — is almost careless, and that carelessness is what Daphne brings to an end.
